terms.meaning: an online service that stores app data in database tables
database rules that limit which rows a given key can see
named values, such as keys and addresses, that the program reads when it starts

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Loads settings and the database client
sections.what: Loads the Next.js environment settings from the project folder, then imports the shared Supabase client used by the app.
sections.why: The settings must exist before the client can connect.
sections.watch_out: Import statements can run before the settings load, and it is unclear from the code whether this file's order avoids that problem.

sections.name: tables
sections.title: List of tables to check
sections.what: Lists every table name the app uses, from profiles to certifications.
sections.why: Gives one place to update when a table is added or removed.
sections.watch_out: The list must match the database exactly, or the table shows up as an error.

sections.name: checkTables
sections.title: Counts and samples each table
sections.what: Asks each table for its row count and up to three sample values, using a short label taken from the first available field. Prints a line per table, or the error message if the request fails.
sections.why: Lets a person quickly see which tables have data and which are broken.
sections.watch_out: Access rules can hide rows, so a table can look empty even when it holds data.

summary: Counts the rows in each Supabase table and prints a few sample names or IDs from each.
purpose: Gives a quick overview of what data is stored in the database.
why: Reason not stated in the code. Likely reason: to confirm each table exists and has data after a migration.
how: Load the environment settings the same way the Next.js app does. Import the Supabase client. Loop through the table names. Ask each table for its row count and a sample. Print a count, a sample, or the error for each table.
inputs: The Supabase settings in the environment, and the fixed list of table names.
outputs: One printed line per table with its count or error, and a few sample values.
risks: Row-level security rules can hide rows from this client, so a zero count may be misleading. Table names must match the database exactly.
debug: If every table errors, check the environment settings and the key. If a single table errors, check its name in the list. If counts look too low, check the access rules on the database.
